intro: Deep in Çorum province, at Ortaköy, lies Sapinuwa, an ancient city of the 14th century BC. This was a Hittite religious and administrative city, and from its ground have come thousands of cuneiform tablets. Let us step into the world that wrote them.
history: Excavations here have run since 1990, led by Aygül and Mustafa Süel. What they uncovered was a royal residence: in the 14th century BC, during the reign of Tudhaliya II, the city served the king. It covered about 9 km², making it one of the largest cities of the ancient Near East. And its thousands of tablets? They survived because a fire baked them hard.
structure-1: You are now standing at Building A, the archive building of Sapinuwa. It was here that the cuneiform tablets were found. Pause for a moment and imagine the clay records gathered within these walls, waiting to be read.
structure-2: Next comes Building B, the storehouse building of Sapinuwa. Picture the goods of a busy royal city kept safe here.
structure-3: Now look for the building with the orthostats. Its orthostat slabs are carved with reliefs in the Hittite Yazılıkaya style, so take a moment to let your eyes follow the figures in the stone.
structure-4: Here are the ritual areas: spaces set apart for worship and ceremonies. Stand quietly for a moment and picture the rites that once unfolded in this place.
structure-5: Sapinuwa was a city on two tiers: the upper city, the elevated citadel, and the lower city, the settlement spread below it. As you look around, try to picture how the two halves fitted together into one city.
facts: Did you know? Building A alone has yielded over 3,000 tablets and fragments, written in Hittite, Hurrian, Akkadian and other languages, among them many Hurrian purification rituals. Because Hittite kings resided here, some scholars count Sapinuwa a second capital. In all, counting those found outside Building A, the excavations have produced more than four thousand cuneiform tablets and fragments. And here is the twist: the fire that destroyed the palace baked the clay tablets hard, so instead of destroying the archive, it carried it down to us.
outro: Our tour of Sapinuwa ends here. Please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. The tablets of this city waited a long time to speak; let its stones wait just as patiently for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
